Curt Delaney, employment counsel. I have got twenty minutes. You are opening Austin and Sacramento, is that right?
That is right. We are opening Austin in March and Sacramento in September. Eleven roles in the first ramp-up, mostly field engineers.

Then you are dealing with two different worlds, and I would not use the same paperwork in both. Start with the easy one. In Texas, employment is at-will and stays at-will unless you write something that changes it.
And in California?

At-will as well, on paper. In practice California gives the employee a great deal more, and a non-compete that is routine in Texas is generally unenforceable there. Do not copy the Texas contract across.
Understood. What is the mistake you see most often with field engineers?

Classification. Somebody decides an engineer is exempt because they are salaried, and two years later there is a claim for unpaid overtime with interest. Send me the job descriptions before you post anything.
I will have them with you by Thursday. And by June we will have hired eight of the eleven, so I would rather be wrong now than in June.

The mistake people from outside the United States make is to think of us as one jurisdiction. We are fifty, plus the federal layer on top, plus cities that make their own rules about pay and about what you may ask a candidate. So the honest answer to almost every question you will ask me is, it depends where. Take notice. There is no statutory notice period in most states, which surprises everybody from Latin America and from Europe. Take non-competes. Routine in Texas, generally unenforceable in California, and the federal position has moved twice in three years. Take pay transparency. In Colorado and in New York you must put a salary range in the advertisement, and in other states you may not even ask what somebody earned before. What I tell every new client is the same thing. Do not build one process. Build one process and a compliance column, and put the state at the top of every page.

We told the board the site would be at full capacity in six weeks and it took seven months. I want to be precise about where the time went, because it was not where anybody expected. Recruiting was not the problem. We filled nine of the eleven roles inside two months. What we had not planned for was that none of the nine could work unaccompanied for another four months, because the certification is site specific and the training slots are booked a quarter ahead. Nobody asked that question, including me. The second thing is that we were running two payrolls in two states with one person who had only ever run one, and by month three she was doing nothing else. If I did it again I would say seven months at the start and I would take the argument in week one, when it costs an uncomfortable meeting, instead of in month four, when it costs your credibility.
